Ohio property tax FAQ

When is the Board of Revision complaint deadline?

Under ORC 5715.19, complaints are due by March 31 or the close of first-half collection, whichever is later, according to the statute text the research opened.

Who sets the value that an Ohio tax bill rests on?

Each county auditor appraises the parcels in that county, and the bill is built on the auditor's figure. The Department of Taxation's resource page describes a complete reappraisal on a six-year cycle, with a lighter triennial update in between that leans on sales data instead of a site visit.

A millage rate then converts value into dollars. Inside mills come from local governments without a ballot, and outside mills come from levies voters approved for schools, fire districts and similar services. This explains why a bill can climb while a house keeps its old value: a new levy lifts the rate. Only the value can be contested before the Board of Revision, never the rate.

The Department of Taxation property tax page outlines two ways to question the figure. A number of counties run an informal review, mostly during reappraisal years, and every county accepts the formal complaint. Call the auditor to learn which applies to your parcel.

How are Ohio tax payments scheduled, and what do late ones cost?

Ohio lets a bill be settled in one payment or two. Under R.C. 323.12, a one-time payment is due by the last day of December, while a half payment (plus any older delinquency) is due then and the remainder on June 20 of the next year. Real bills often show later dates, since R.C. 323.17 pushes payment out to January 31 and July 20 whenever the duplicate reaches the treasurer late. Trust the dates printed on your own bill.

The treasurer must receive a payment by the last day, or it must carry a U.S. Postal Service postmark from that day or earlier. Stamps from a private postage meter are no good for this purpose, and a treasurer may hold the books open briefly to process what came in.

The penalty schedule in R.C. 323.121 works like this:

  • Miss the first-half deadline and the unpaid half picks up a ten percent charge.
  • Miss the second-half deadline and the remaining unpaid current taxes pick up another ten percent charge.
  • Back taxes then accrue interest at the rate fixed under section 5703.47.

How do I contest my valuation with the Board of Revision?

Paperwork starts at the auditor's counter, and the auditor hands it on to the Board of Revision. Under R.C. 5715.19 the window closes on whichever comes second: the end of March after the tax year in question, or the day the treasurer finishes collecting first-half payments. Postmarks decide timeliness for mail.

Besides the owner, the statute names the owner's spouse, a retained assessment professional, a retained accountant, appraiser or real estate broker, and in some commercial leases the tenant. Gather comparable sales, an independent appraisal if you hold one, and photographs of the house as it stands.

A repeat complaint is blocked inside one interim period unless something new happened after the lien date. The statute lists what counts:

  • An arm's length sale of the property.
  • A casualty loss of value.
  • A substantial improvement.
  • An occupancy change of fifteen percent or more that hits the property's economics hard.

An unhappy result can go to the Board of Tax Appeals. R.C. 5717.01 gives thirty days from the mailing of the county board's notice.

What does the Ohio homestead exemption give a qualifying owner?

It lowers the tax on a home the owner lives in. R.C. 323.152 reaches people who are permanently and totally disabled, people at least sixty-five, some surviving spouses, disabled veterans, and surviving spouses of public service officers killed on duty. Under R.C. 323.151, the protected home takes in as much as one acre around the dwelling, and the age test is met by anyone who reached sixty-four before January 1 of the application year.

The base reduction shields twenty-five thousand dollars of true value, indexed to inflation by the tax commissioner. Disabled veterans and the surviving spouses of officers killed on duty get fifty thousand dollars and face no income test. Other applicants must stay under an income ceiling that the statute states as thirty thousand dollars of total income, also indexed yearly. The auditor can give the current number.

A second layer applies to any homestead. The text lists percentages of the tax from qualifying levies: 5.70 percent for the first tax year the amendment applies, 8.92 percent, 12.15 percent, and then 15.38 percent for the third following year and later. Ask the auditor which step your year falls on.

Filing happens at the auditor's office. The Department of Taxation names form DTE 105A for most people, DTE 105I for disabled veterans and their surviving spouses, and DTE 105K for officers' surviving spouses. After approval an owner stays enrolled unless eligibility changes. A different benefit, the owner-occupancy credit, covers a primary residence lived in on January 1 of the application year.

How does unpaid tax affect the sale of an Ohio house?

The year's tax lien attaches to the real property on January 1 and stays until tax, penalties and interest are paid, as R.C. 323.11 puts it. Transferring the deed does not wipe it out, so the amount owed must come out of the sale money or the buyer inherits it. Ask the county treasurer for a payoff amount before the closing date.

The deed stage adds a form. Under R.C. 319.202, the buyer files a statement of value with the auditor, and it has to address whether the seller's taxes were reduced by the homestead exemption and whether the land was valued for current agricultural use. A buyer who does not qualify for a reduction the seller enjoyed should expect the next bill to differ.

An owner already behind has an exit from foreclosure. R.C. 323.31 guarantees an occupant owner one written delinquent tax contract with the county treasurer. A home in that position gets up to five years of installments, and at least two if the owner asks. A missed installment or unpaid current tax voids the deal, and none is available while a tax certificate or foreclosure judgment stands.

More questions about Ohio Property Tax Guide

When is the Ohio Board of Revision complaint deadline?

Whichever is later: the end of March after the tax year, or the day first-half collection ends. Hand the complaint to the auditor, whose office passes it along. If you mail it, the postmark date is what counts.

Does Ohio let me pay property tax in installments?

Yes. The statute allows two halves, one around year end and one in June, and a late duplicate pushes both into January and July. The dates printed on your bill control.

Can I get a homestead exemption if I am under sixty-five?

Yes, if you are permanently and totally disabled on January 1 of the application year, or if you are a disabled veteran or a qualifying surviving spouse. The statute also provides a partial exemption on any homestead. Apply through the county auditor.

Who sets the Ohio millage rate?

Local governments set inside mills, and voters approve outside mills through levies. The rate cannot be changed by a valuation complaint. Only the property's value can be challenged at the Board of Revision.

What if I cannot pay my Ohio property tax on a home I live in?

Ask the county treasurer about a delinquent tax contract. An owner who lives in the home is entitled to one, payable over up to five years. Entering it before a foreclosure judgment keeps the county from filing suit while installments are paid.

Ohio homestead exemption FAQ

Where do I apply for the homestead exemption?

With the county auditor. Filing dates and forms are set locally.

Who qualifies for the Ohio homestead exemption?

Ohio gives the exemption to owner-occupants who are 65 or older, permanently and totally disabled, or the surviving spouse of someone in those groups. Disabled veterans, their surviving spouses, and surviving spouses of public service officers killed in the line of duty have their own larger reduction. The definitions sit in R.C. 323.151.

Age is counted in a specific way. For this purpose, 'sixty-five years of age or older' means a person who reached 64 before January 1 of the year of application. The Department of Taxation adds that a senior owner must be 65 by December 31 of the year the application is filed.

The home itself has to meet several tests:

  • It is a dwelling the applicant owns and occupies as a home, with Ohio as the domicile.
  • It includes the surrounding land only up to one acre that is reasonably needed for the home.
  • It was not acquired from a relative, other than a spouse, for the purpose of qualifying.
  • An owner can be a life tenant, a vendee in possession under a land contract, a mortgagor, or the settlor of a trust that holds title to a home the settlor occupies.

The Department of Taxation notes that homes held by corporations, partnerships and LLCs generally do not qualify, because the owner is not an individual.

How much does the exemption take off an Ohio tax bill?

It takes the form of a credit on the property tax bill, calculated on a slice of the home's market value. The size of the credit also depends on the local tax rate: the Department of Taxation says that the higher the rate, the higher the credit. The reduction amounts are indexed for inflation each year.

Homestead reduction amounts and income limit printed by the Ohio Department of Taxation (real property)
ItemTax year 2025Tax year 2026
Low-income senior or disabled owner$29,000$29,700
Disabled veteran, or surviving spouse of a public service officer killed in the line of duty$58,000$59,400
Income threshold for seniors and disabled owners$40,000$41,000

Source: Ohio Department of Taxation, Homestead Means Testing FAQ. Income is measured by modified adjusted gross income, which the statute defines for the owner and spouse for the year before the application.

No income test applies to disabled veterans, their surviving spouses, or the surviving spouses of public service officers. Owners who received the exemption in 2013, before means testing returned, are also outside the income test.

Where and when do you file in Ohio?

File with the county auditor of the county where the home sits, on or before December 31 of the year the reduction is sought. The Department of Taxation lists three forms: DTE 105A for most applicants, DTE 105I for disabled veterans and their surviving spouses, and DTE 105K for surviving spouses of public service officers. Every county auditor must take a paper copy, and some accept electronic filing.

A disability claim needs a certificate. R.C. 323.153 calls for a physician's certificate for a physical disability, and a physician or psychologist licensed in Ohio for a mental one. A certificate from a state or federal agency that classifies disability also works. Veterans attach written confirmation from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs.

After filing, the sequence runs like this:

  • The auditor approves or denies the application and sends notice within thirty days of that decision.
  • A denial notice must state the reasons.
  • An owner who thinks the denial was wrong, or the reduction too small, can appeal to the county board of revision within sixty days of the notice, using form DTE 106B.
  • Each January the auditor mails a continuing application. Send it back only if ownership, occupancy, disability or income changed.

A false statement made to get the reduction is a fourth-degree misdemeanor and bars the reduction for three years after a conviction.

What happens to the exemption when an Ohio owner sells?

The reduction follows the owner, not the house. Under R.C. 323.152(C), a transfer of ownership after an application was filed does not forfeit the reduction for that year. Once the home is sold, though, the seller no longer owns or occupies it, so the continuing application should be returned to the auditor reporting the change.

Failure to report has a price. If the auditor or treasurer finds that an owner kept a reduction after losing eligibility, a charge goes on the property for each affected tax year, with interest as if the reduction were delinquent tax. That charge is collected like delinquent taxes, which makes it a closing item for a title company to catch.

The buyer starts from a different place. The partial exemption for homesteads in R.C. 323.152(B)(2) calls for a fresh application when a home changed hands in the preceding year, and the auditor mails an original application each February for homes that transferred. The filing deadline is again December 31. A senior or disabled buyer who moves in must apply at the new address, and the Department of Taxation says to begin in January of the year after the move. Ownership and occupancy as of January 1 decide the tax year.

What other Ohio property tax reductions sit next to the homestead exemption?

Three other pieces of relief show up on Ohio residential bills. The first is the partial exemption under R.C. 319.302, which the auditor reviews parcel by parcel as of January 1. For residential property it is listed at seven and one-half percent for the first tax year the amendment applies, with later steps ending at zero percent for and after the third following tax year. Ask the auditor what percentage applies to a given bill.

The second is the owner-occupancy credit, which the Department of Taxation describes as a reduction on a primary residence occupied on January 1 of the application year. Owners should ask the auditor whether it already appears on their bill.

The third is a county option created by House Bill 96, signed in June 2025. County commissioners may adopt a local-option homestead exemption that mirrors the state one, with the same eligibility rules and the same amount. Nobody applies for it separately: anyone already getting the state exemption receives it automatically once a county turns it on. Whether a given county has done so is a question for the auditor.

Farmland has its own track, the Current Agricultural Use Value program, which also runs through the auditor.

Does the exemption change how an Ohio house sells?

It rarely changes the sale itself, but it affects the tax figures on the settlement statement. A seller who has been receiving the credit should bring the most recent tax bill to the closing, since the credit shows there. A buyer who plans to live in the house should ask the title company how the owner-occupancy filing is handled at the county auditor's conveyance step.

A few practical points for sellers:

  • An heir who inherits a home does not get the seller's reduction automatically. Eligibility depends on the new owner's own age, disability and occupancy.
  • A home under a land contract can still qualify, because R.C. 323.151 counts a vendee in possession as an owner.
  • Pending appeals and unpaid installments are matters for the county treasurer, who bills and collects the tax.

Selling a house with back taxes, a tenant, or heavy repairs is a different problem from the exemption. A direct sale to a cash buyer skips showings and repair negotiations, and the title company still handles any tax proration at closing.

More questions about Ohio Homestead Exemption

Do I have to reapply for the Ohio homestead exemption every year?

No. Once approved, the application continues for each year the dwelling is your homestead. The auditor mails a continuing application each January, and you return it only if your income, ownership, occupancy or disability status changed.

What is the last day to file the Ohio homestead exemption for real property?

December 31 of the year the reduction is sought. Manufactured and mobile homes taxed that way file by December 31 of the year before. The statute allows a late application for the preceding year to be filed with an original application.

Can I get the Ohio homestead exemption if my home is in a trust?

Often yes. The Department of Taxation says revocable and irrevocable trusts can qualify when the trust gives you complete possession of the property. Check the trust language with the county auditor before applying.

Who decides the Ohio homestead exemption, and where do I appeal?

The county auditor decides it. If you believe the denial or the amount is wrong, file a complaint with the county board of revision within sixty days of the auditor's notice.

Does selling my Ohio home end the exemption?

Yes, for future years. The reduction applies to a home you own and occupy, so tell the auditor when you no longer qualify. Skipping that step can lead to a charge on the property with interest for years the reduction should not have been given.

What the official sources say

  • When a mortgage is foreclosed, a sale of the property shall be ordered by the court of common pleas having jurisdiction; court may order sale in parcels or as a whole. (ORC 2323.07 (eff. Sept. 11, 2008); source)
  • Sheriff calls three disinterested freeholders to appraise land levied upon; for residential property they must return an estimate within 21 calendar days of the clerk's order of appraisal. (ORC 2329.17(A)-(B) (eff. Mar. 20, 2019); source)
  • Court examines the sale and, if proper, within 30 days of return of the writ journalizes satisfaction and orders title transferred to purchaser (confirmation). (ORC 2329.31(A) (eff. Sept. 29, 2017); source)
  • Debtor may redeem from a sale at any time before confirmation by depositing with the clerk the judgment amount, costs, and 8% per annum interest on purchase money; there is no post-confirmation redemption right. (ORC 2329.33 (eff. Sept. 28, 2016); source)

What we could not confirm

  • Post-confirmation redemption is not expressly stated in the statute text opened.

How does an Ohio foreclosure end in a sheriff sale?

A lender files a foreclosure suit in the county court of common pleas, wins a judgment, and the court orders the property sold. R.C. 2323.07 says the court may order a tract sold whole or in parcels, and where land lies in several counties it may direct the sheriff of each county or one officer to sell it. The sale itself is then run under Chapter 2329.

The Supreme Court of Ohio's foreclosure mediation guide warns that once a borrower receives notice of the lawsuit, the home could be lost in three to six months. It advises opening every piece of mail from the court, contacting the servicer right away, and staying in the house. Occupancy is advised because the home stays in better condition and the lender prefers it that way until the sheriff says otherwise.

Hotlines listed on the Ohio Attorney General's foreclosure page include Save the Dream Ohio at 888-404-4674, the Ohio Department of Commerce at 800-750-0750, Ohio State Legal Services Association at 866-529-6446 and HUD approved counselors at 888-995-HOPE.

How is an Ohio house appraised before the sheriff sells it?

The sheriff calls three disinterested freeholders, who must live in the county and own real property there, to appraise the land on actual view. Under R.C. 2329.17, for a residence they have twenty-one calendar days from the clerk's order to return a value. If they miss that window, the freeholders are not paid, the appraised value becomes the auditor's most recent value, and the sale moves ahead. A court can approve a separate appraisal for good cause.

The same section lets the municipality or township inspect any structures on the land before the sale. Ask the sheriff's office whether an inspection has been scheduled for your property.

The appraisal sets the floor for the first auction. Under R.C. 2329.20, land may not be sold for less than two-thirds of its appraised value, with exceptions in sections 2329.51 and 2329.52. A junior lien holder enforcing against land subject to a prior lien faces a modified minimum figure, set by the court.

What notice does an Ohio sheriff sale require?

Two kinds of notice are needed. R.C. 2329.26 requires the creditor or its attorney to serve a written notice on the judgment debtor and each other party, and to file that notice with proof of service at least seven calendar days before the sale. A party in default for failing to appear in the case does not have to be served. The officer must also advertise the sale once a week for at least three consecutive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation in the county.

The advertisement states the date, time and place, or for an online sale the start date, minimum duration and web address. It also states the required deposit and tells bidders they answer for costs, allowances and taxes the proceeds do not cover.

These rules have teeth. Under R.C. 2329.27, a sale made without the required notices is set aside on motion of an interested party. Once the court confirms a sale, though, that order is treated as a finding that notice was adequate and bars further motions to set the sale aside. A homeowner who spots a notice defect needs to raise it before confirmation.

What are the deposit and second auction rules?

A bidder other than the foreclosing lender must put down a deposit set by the home's appraised value. R.C. 2329.211 sets three tiers for residential property:

  • Two thousand dollars when the appraisal is ten thousand dollars or less.
  • Five thousand dollars when the appraisal is above ten thousand and up to two hundred thousand.
  • Ten thousand dollars when the appraisal is above two hundred thousand.

A purchaser who misses the deposit timing makes the sale invalid, and the home can go to a provisional second sale if one was announced.

If a house in a residential mortgage foreclosure fails to sell at the first auction, R.C. 2329.52 calls for a second auction between seven and thirty days later. That auction goes to the highest bidder with no minimum bid, though costs, allowances and real estate taxes still have to be covered. A house still unsold after two auctions may be offered again without the minimum or disposed of in another way allowed by the chapter.

What are the steps from judgment to deed, and what do they say?

The table lays out the statutory sequence a homeowner can watch on the court docket.

AppraisalThree freeholders, 21 days for a home2329.17
Minimum bid, first auctionTwo-thirds of appraised value2329.20
Public noticeWeekly for at least three consecutive weeks2329.26
Second auction7 to 30 days later, no minimum bid2329.52
ConfirmationWithin 30 days of return of the writ2329.31
RedemptionAny time before confirmation2329.33

Everything in the table is taken from the Ohio Revised Code at codes.ohio.gov.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Ohio houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Can I redeem or stop an Ohio sheriff sale?

Yes, until the court confirms the sale. R.C. 2329.33 lets the debtor deposit with the clerk the judgment amount, all costs, and interest at eight percent a year on the purchase money from the day of sale. The court then sets the sale aside, applies the deposit to the judgment and awards the interest to the bidder. After confirmation, redemption under that section is gone.

Timing is tight. R.C. 2329.31 says the court reviews the sale and journalizes confirmation within thirty days of the return of the writ, though it may stay confirmation to let an owner redeem. The buyer then has thirty days after confirmation to pay the balance, and the officer records the deed within fourteen days after confirmation and payment. If the deed is late, the buyer can ask for a court order that works as the deed. The county auditor then updates ownership for tax purposes, and taxes coming due after the sale fall on the new owner.

A sale of the house itself can produce the redemption money. Ask the plaintiff's attorney for a written payoff, check the docket with the clerk, and keep the confirmation date in view.

Mediation is another route. The Supreme Court's guide says a foreclosure case can be mediated from before filing up to confirmation of the sale, and that even after the sheriff sale it has been done. Programs vary by county court, so call the court. After a sale, the guide describes the general order of payment as the court, the sheriff, the county treasurer, then lien holders, with any remainder going to the owner. The guide also warns that some firms charge fees for services that are available for free, and that Save the Dream Ohio referrals cost nothing.

More questions about Ohio Sheriff Sale

How long does a sheriff sale take after a foreclosure judgment in Ohio?

The statutes set pieces, not one total. Appraisal takes up to twenty-one days, advertising runs at least three weeks, confirmation follows within thirty days of the writ's return, and the buyer has thirty days to pay. Ask the clerk for the dates on your case.

What is the minimum bid at an Ohio sheriff sale?

Two-thirds of the appraised value at the first auction. For a residential mortgage foreclosure, a second auction held seven to thirty days later has no minimum bid. Costs and real estate taxes still have to be covered.

Can I redeem my Ohio home after the sheriff sale?

Only before the court confirms the sale. You deposit the judgment amount, costs and eight percent interest on the purchase money with the clerk. Once confirmed, that right ends.

Do I have to move out before the Ohio sheriff sale?

No. The Supreme Court of Ohio's guide urges owners to stay in the home and keep it in good condition until the sheriff says they must leave.

Where can I get free help with an Ohio foreclosure?

Call Save the Dream Ohio at 888-404-4674, or the Ohio State Legal Services Association at 866-529-6446. HUD approved counselors are at 888-995-HOPE. Your county common pleas court can tell you whether it offers foreclosure mediation.

Ohio estate tax FAQ

Does Ohio have an estate tax?

The Department of Taxation says the estate tax was repealed for deaths on or after January 1, 2013.

Does Ohio charge an estate tax?

No. The Ohio Department of Taxation reports that House Bill 153 repealed the state estate tax for every estate with a date of death in 2013 or later. House Bill 110 of the 134th General Assembly then added a sunset for the older estates: nothing is owed on property first discovered after December 31, 2021, or on property found earlier but never disclosed or reported by that date.

So an Ohio family selling an inherited house does not file a state estate tax return before closing. The Department also says it has dropped the requirement for ET 12, 13 and 14 release forms before a decedent's assets move to another person, and it asked county auditors and banks to stop forwarding them.

Could the federal estate tax reach an Ohio estate?

Only a very large one. For deaths in 2026 the IRS lists $15,000,000 as the basic exclusion amount, raised by Public Law 119-21, which was signed July 4, 2025. A single house rarely comes near that line, so for most families the federal return does not set the timeline.

The IRS adds two points. An estate that does not have to file a federal return should skip Form 8971, and the estate of someone survived by a spouse may elect to pass unused exclusion to that spouse on a timely filed return.

Who signs the deed when an inherited Ohio house is sold?

Usually the executor or administrator, under the supervision of the probate court that serves the decedent's home county. Ohio's land-sale procedure for executors, administrators and guardians runs from R.C. 2127.01 through 2127.43, and an executor whose will grants a power of sale may follow the will instead.

Smaller estates may not need full administration. Under R.C. 2113.03 the court can release an estate from administration at $35,000 in assets or under, or up to $100,000 when a surviving spouse takes everything. The order can direct delivery of personal property and transfer of real property, and the court may appoint a commissioner to sign the conveyance papers. A buyer who pays value in good faith gets the same protection from unsecured creditors that administration would give.

  • Ask the probate clerk whether the estate fits a release or needs letters of authority.
  • Gather the death certificate, the will, and the vesting deed.
  • Order a title search early so liens surface before a buyer finds them.

What changes if the owner recorded a transfer on death affidavit?

Title may already sit with the named beneficiary. R.C. 5302.22 lets an owner sign a verified transfer on death designation affidavit and record it with the county recorder before death. At the owner's death, title vests in the beneficiaries the affidavit names.

The affidavit needs neither payment nor delivery to work, and the recorder charges the deed fee and indexes it under the owner's name. Heirs who suspect a parent signed one should ask the recorder to search that name. Knowingly false statements in the affidavit are falsification under R.C. 2921.13.

What tax do heirs face when they sell an inherited Ohio house?

The IRS measures gain from the heir's basis, which for inherited property generally equals the fair market value at the date of death. Estates that elected the alternate valuation date use that figure, and farm or business land can use special-use valuation. Publication 551 says an heir who received no Schedule A (Form 8971) from the executor can rely on the appraised date-of-death value used for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes.

That makes an early appraisal worth ordering. Keep it with the estate papers so the tax preparer can apply it to the final price.

Can an heir challenge the county's value of the house?

An owner can. R.C. 5715.19 sends a valuation complaint to the county auditor, with a filing deadline of March 31 of the following tax year unless first-half collection closes later. The county board of revision decides it, and the statute limits repeat complaints on one parcel within the same interim period unless something changed, such as an arm's length sale, a casualty loss or a substantial improvement.

A date-of-death appraisal can back up a complaint when the county figure looks high. The auditor's office can say which tax year a new filing would cover.

What will a buyer and title company ask the estate to provide?

Expect requests for proof of who has authority to sign, because a title company will not insure a deed it cannot trace. For an estate in administration that means the executor's or administrator's letters of authority from the probate court. For a released estate it means a copy of the release order. For a house covered by a transfer on death affidavit, it means the recorded affidavit and a death certificate.

The title company also searches for mortgages, judgments and unpaid tax. Because Ohio land sales by fiduciaries follow the statute, a sale that skips the court steps can leave a buyer with a cloud on title. If the file is complicated, a probate attorney in the home county can confirm which documents the closing will need before you accept an offer.

What should an Ohio heir do first?

Begin with whatever decides who may sign, then turn to the house. The probate clerk is the first call.

  • Find the original will and file it with the probate court if no one has.
  • Keep the house insured and secured, and redirect the mail.
  • Ask the recorder whether a transfer on death affidavit exists.
  • Request the current tax bill from the county treasurer.
  • Order the date-of-death appraisal.

An estate that needs to move quickly sometimes sells to a buyer who purchases without repairs or showings. If that fits, compare offers on what the estate keeps after transfer tax, payoffs and costs, since those items apply whichever way the house sells.

More questions about Ohio Estate Tax

Does Ohio have an estate tax in 2026?

No. The Ohio Department of Taxation says the tax was repealed for estates with a 2013 or later date of death, and the House Bill 110 sunset ended collection on property first discovered after December 31, 2021.

Do I need a state tax release to transfer a parent's Ohio house?

No. The Department of Taxation says it no longer requires the ET 12, 13 or 14 release forms. Title and probate steps still apply, so ask the probate court clerk what the estate needs.

Is there a federal estate tax on a modest Ohio estate?

Not at that size. The IRS lists $15,000,000 as the federal basic exclusion amount for 2026 deaths and $13,990,000 for 2025 deaths, and estates under that amount are not required to file Form 706 for that reason.

Can a house pass without full probate in Ohio?

Sometimes. A recorded transfer on death affidavit vests title in the named beneficiary under R.C. 5302.22, and a probate court can release an estate with $35,000 or less in assets under R.C. 2113.03. The probate court can tell you which path fits.

Who pays the county transfer tax when an estate sells in Ohio?

The seller named in the deed. R.C. 322.02 puts the charge on the grantor, payable to the county auditor before the deed reaches the recorder, at a rate each county sets within the thirty-cent cap.

What the official sources say

  • If vendee has paid for five years or more or has paid 20% or more of the price, vendor can recover possession only via foreclosure and judicial sale under ORC 2323.07. (ORC 5313.07 (eff. Nov. 25, 1969); source)
  • Forfeiture notice to a defaulting vendee must state the contract is forfeited unless performed within ten days of completed service and tell vendee to leave. (ORC 5313.06(C); source)

What we could not confirm

Ohio land contract FAQ

What is a land contract?

A contract where the buyer pays in installments and the seller keeps legal title until a set point. Chapter 5313 of the Ohio Revised Code governs them.

What counts as a land installment contract in Ohio?

In Ohio it is an executory agreement, not fully performed within a year, under which the seller agrees to convey title and the buyer pays the price in installments while the seller keeps title as security. Chapter 5313 of the Revised Code covers it, and R.C. 5313.01 sets the terms. The chapter speaks of a vendor (seller) and a vendee (buyer).

Two limits in the definitions matter. The property must be real property in Ohio improved by a dwelling, so a bare lot sale does not fall under the chapter. And an option contract to buy real property is expressly not a land installment contract.

Ohio lets the seller be almost anyone: an individual, partnership, corporation, association, trust, or any other group. An investor who sells on contract is covered by the same chapter as a homeowner who sells to a neighbor.

What must an Ohio land contract say?

The contract is signed in duplicate, and each side gets a copy. R.C. 5313.02 then lists sixteen items the document must contain at a minimum.

  • Full names and current mailing addresses of all parties, and the date each party signed.
  • A legal description of the property, the contract price, any separate service charges, the down payment, and the resulting principal balance.
  • The amount and due date of each installment, plus the interest rate on the unpaid balance and how it is computed.
  • A statement of encumbrances against the property and of any pending order of a public agency.
  • A promise to deliver a general warranty deed on completion, or another available deed if a general warranty deed is not possible.
  • A provision that the seller supply evidence of title under local custom.
  • A provision that, if the seller defaults on a mortgage, the buyer may pay it and get credit on the contract.
  • A provision that the seller will have the contract recorded, and a term making the buyer responsible for taxes and assessments from the contract date unless the parties agree otherwise.

The seller cannot carry a mortgage larger than the balance due on the contract, unless the mortgage covers additional property and the seller disclosed the amount and release price in writing. A seller also cannot place a larger mortgage without the buyer's consent. If the legal description is by metes and bounds, the county engineer reviews it and marks approval on the contract.

When must an Ohio land contract be recorded?

Within twenty days after both parties sign, the seller must cause a copy to be recorded under R.C. 5301.25 and deliver a copy to the county auditor. Recording puts the buyer's interest on the public record at the county recorder, which matters if the seller later sells or borrows against the same house.

The contract must also follow the formalities that Ohio law requires for deeds and mortgages. Each county recorder keeps its own fee schedule and filing instructions, so ask the recorder where the property sits for current requirements.

The chapter adds an ongoing duty. At least once a year, or on the buyer's demand but no more than twice a year, the seller must furnish a statement showing the amount credited to principal and interest and the balance due. A land contract passbook issued by the seller or a financial institution satisfies this. If a seller ignores the chapter, R.C. 5313.04 lets the buyer enforce it in a municipal court, county court or court of common pleas.

What can an Ohio seller do when the buyer stops paying?

Start by waiting out the cure period. Under R.C. 5313.05, forfeiture can be enforced only after thirty days from the date of default, and a buyer who pays everything currently due, with any charges, inside that window avoids forfeiture.

After the thirty days, the seller serves a written notice. Under R.C. 5313.06 it must identify the contract and the property, list the terms not met, and say the contract stands forfeited unless the buyer performs within ten days of completed service. It must also tell the buyer to leave. Service can be by hand, by leaving it at the usual home or at the property, or by registered or certified mail to the last known address.

The route after that depends on how far the buyer has paid:

  • Under five years in, the seller may sue for forfeiture and restitution of the property under Chapter 1923, and serving the 5313.06 notice satisfies the three-day notice rule in R.C. 1923.04(A).
  • At five years of payments, or twenty percent of the price paid, the seller can recover possession only through foreclosure and a judicial sale under R.C. 2323.07.
  • In that sale the seller takes proceeds up to the unpaid contract balance.

A judgment for the seller cancels the contract as of a date the court sets. The court clerk sends a certified copy to the county recorder, who records it as an instrument of cancellation. Choosing to end the contract this way is the seller's exclusive remedy, with one exception: if the buyer paid less than fair rental value plus damage to the property, the seller may recover the difference.

Source for every row: the section of the Ohio Revised Code named in the last column, on codes.ohio.gov. A seller who wants to end a contract should confirm each period against the current statute text.

What disclosures and sale issues come up on an Ohio land contract house?

The residential property disclosure form in R.C. 5302.30 applies to transfers of one-to-four unit residential property made by sale, land installment contract, lease with option to purchase, exchange, or a 99-year renewable lease. A seller on contract completes and delivers the form to the prospective buyer as soon as practicable. The statute exempts transfers by court order, by a fiduciary administering an estate, between spouses or to lineal relatives, to a buyer who has lived in the property for a year or more, and a few others.

If the buyer gets the form or an amendment after signing, the buyer has three business days to rescind in writing, and the right ends by the earlier of thirty days after acceptance or closing. A buyer who never receives the form after making an offer may also rescind within that same outer limit.

Owners who want out of a land contract situation have a few starting points. A seller who holds title and wants to sell the house outright will need the recorded contract, the payment history, and the mortgage payoff. A buyer in default who has paid for several years should talk to a lawyer before leaving, since the five-year and twenty-percent rules can change what the seller may do. Both sides can also cancel their interest together by an instrument recorded under R.C. 5301.331, which Chapter 5313 expressly leaves available.

More questions about Ohio Land Contracts

How long does an Ohio land contract buyer have to cure a missed payment?

Thirty days from the date of default. Paying all amounts currently due plus any contract fees within that period stops forfeiture, per R.C. 5313.05.

Can an Ohio seller evict a land contract buyer who has paid for years?

Not by forfeiture alone once the buyer has paid for five years or has paid twenty percent of the price. At that point the seller must use foreclosure and judicial sale under R.C. 2323.07.

Does an Ohio land contract have to be recorded?

Yes. The seller must cause a copy to be recorded and delivered to the county auditor within twenty days after both parties sign, according to R.C. 5313.02(C).

What notice does an Ohio seller give before forfeiture?

A written notice that names the contract and property, lists the unmet terms, says the contract is forfeited unless the buyer performs within ten days of service, and tells the buyer to leave. R.C. 5313.06 sets those contents.

Can I rent out or sell a house I am buying on land contract in Ohio?

That depends on the contract terms and the seller's recorded title, which Chapter 5313 leaves to the written agreement. Ask a real estate attorney and the county recorder before listing.

What the official sources say

  • To begin an eviction (forcible entry and detainer) action, the party must give the adverse party notice to leave at least three days before filing, by certified mail, hand delivery, or leaving at the abode/premises, except as provided in (B) or (C). (ORC 1923.04(A) (eff. Oct. 18, 2007); source)

How long does an Ohio eviction take from filing to move-out?

Ohio Legal Help says an eviction is a process that can take four to six weeks, so a tenant's belongings are not set out the next day. Once a landlord files, the court sends a summons and the hearing usually falls about two weeks later.

Cold weather does not pause the case. The same guide states that a tenant can be evicted in Ohio even in winter. For an owner who plans to sell, that four to six week stretch begins only after the written notice has run, so the calendar from notice to an empty house is longer than the court phase alone.

What are the steps in an Ohio eviction case?

Chapter 1923 of the Revised Code, the forcible entry and detainer chapter, sets the sequence. Each step below leads to the next, and a landlord who skips one risks a dismissal.

  • Written notice to leave, given at least three days before the case begins (R.C. 1923.04).
  • Complaint filed with the municipal or county court that covers the rental address.
  • Summons issued and served, at least seven days before trial (R.C. 1923.06).
  • Hearing before a judge unless a jury is demanded or the case is continued (R.C. 1923.09).
  • Judgment for restitution of the premises plus court costs.
  • Writ of execution requested and carried out by the sheriff, a police officer, a constable or a court bailiff (R.C. 1923.13 and 1923.14).

How is the summons served on an Ohio tenant?

The clerk always mails the summons and a copy of the complaint by ordinary mail, with a certificate of mailing. The plaintiff then picks a second method when filing: personal-type service by a sheriff, a court bailiff or an adult the court designates, or certified mail with return receipt.

The person serving process goes to the rental. If the tenant is there, the papers are handed over. If not, they are left with someone of suitable age and discretion at the address. If neither works, a copy is posted in a conspicuous place on the premises. That person must return the process to the clerk within five days and note which method was used.

Service counts as complete when the first two methods are used, or when ordinary mailing and posting have both happened. The summons itself carries a notice that a tenant depositing rent with the clerk must keep depositing it until the hearing, that a jury trial may be requested, and that free legal help may be available.

What happens at the hearing and what can the judgment include?

If no one asks for a jury or a continuance, a judge tries the case and can reach one of three results under R.C. 1923.09.

  • Complaint true: judgment for restitution of the premises to the landlord, with costs of suit.
  • Complaint true in part: restitution for that part only, with costs divided as the judge sees fit.
  • Complaint not true: judgment against the landlord for costs.

R.C. 1923.081 allows the same trial to include the landlord's claims for past due rent and other damages, unless the court continues those claims for good cause. A tenant's request to file an answer, a counterclaim or to take discovery counts as good cause, and the case then runs like other civil cases. Ohio Legal Help adds that a tenant who needs time to find a lawyer can ask for a continuance, and that agreements reached before the hearing should be in writing and told to the judge.

How does the writ of eviction work after judgment?

After a judgment of restitution, the landlord asks the court to issue a writ of execution. Ohio Legal Help says a red tag is posted on the door telling the tenant how long remains to leave, and that the period is generally five days. After that the landlord can ask the officer to set the tenant's things out.

R.C. 1923.14 says the officer must carry out the writ within ten days after receiving it by restoring the landlord to possession. A tenant who appeals and obtains a stay of execution after posting any required bond can pause the removal, and the judge then orders the officer to delay further proceedings.

How does an eviction affect the sale of a rented Ohio house?

A pending case does not stop an owner from signing a purchase contract, but the buyer cannot take possession until the tenant leaves voluntarily or the writ is carried out. Buyers who want the house vacant will often ask the seller to finish the court process first. Other buyers purchase the house with the tenant in place.

Ohio's self-help ban still applies while the sale is in progress. A landlord may not shut off utilities or lock the tenant out to speed things up (R.C. 5321.15), and a retaliatory possession action can be raised as a defense (R.C. 5321.02).

Manufactured home parks follow their own end steps. If an evicted resident leaves a home unoccupied for three days after judgment, the operator may give the titled owner written notice to remove it within fourteen days. A home worth more than three thousand dollars goes to a sheriff's sale within sixty days of the writ. A home worth three thousand dollars or less can have its title transferred to the plaintiff within thirty days, through the clerk of the common pleas title division.

Where can Ohio landlords and tenants get help with an eviction case?

Start with the clerk of the court named on the summons, who can explain local filing and hearing procedures but cannot give legal advice. Ohio Legal Help lists free legal aid by county, and Akron, Cleveland, Columbus and Toledo have Right to Counsel programs for some tenants with low income. Owners with several rentals often hire a landlord attorney, because a missed deadline can force them to restart the notice and filing sequence. Keep a file with the lease, the rent ledger, the notice, proof of delivery and every court paper, since the judge and the buyer will both ask for them.

More questions about Ohio Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How many days does a tenant have to leave after an Ohio eviction judgment?

Ohio Legal Help says the posted red tag generally allows five days. After that the landlord can ask the sheriff or bailiff to carry out the writ, which the officer must execute within ten days after receiving it.

Can a landlord evict a tenant in the winter in Ohio?

Yes. Ohio Legal Help states that evictions can happen in winter or very cold weather. The case follows the same notice, hearing and writ steps as in any other season.

What is the earliest an Ohio eviction hearing can be held?

No sooner than the seventh day after service of the summons is complete, under R.C. 1923.06(H). Service must be made at least seven days before the day set for trial.

Can a landlord collect back rent in the same Ohio case?

Often yes. R.C. 1923.081 allows the trial to include claims for past due rent and other damages, unless the court continues those claims for good cause such as a tenant's request to answer or take discovery.

Does an eviction filing stop a sale of the house?

No. An owner can still sell, but possession depends on the tenant leaving or the writ being carried out. A buyer who wants a vacant house usually asks the seller to complete the court process before closing.

  • Deeds and instruments conveying land must be recorded with the county recorder where the premises lie; until recorded they are fraudulent as to a subsequent bona fide purchaser without knowledge. (ORC 5301.25(A); source)

Ohio quitclaim deed FAQ

Who pays the Ohio conveyance fee?

ORC 319.202 makes the grantor pay the mandatory fee and any county permissive tax.

What does an Ohio quitclaim deed actually transfer?

It transfers whatever interest the signer has, no more. R.C. 5301.02 says a grant of land conveys the entire interest the grantor could lawfully convey unless the deed clearly shows a smaller estate was intended. A quitclaim does not add anything to that: if the grantor owns half, the grantee gets half.

The Revised Code prints statutory forms for three other deed types, and each one carries named promises. The general warranty form in R.C. 5302.05 brings covenants that the grantor holds the land in fee simple, that it is free of encumbrances and that the grantor will defend title against all claims. The limited warranty form in 5302.07 narrows those promises to claims arising through the grantor. The fiduciary form in 5302.09 is for executors, administrators, trustees, guardians and receivers.

Those covenants arrive only when the deed says so. R.C. 5302.06 gives the words "general warranty covenants" the full meaning of the promises listed there. A deed without such words leaves the buyer relying on the title the grantor really has.

Who can witness the signing of an Ohio deed?

Ohio requires the grantor's signature to be acknowledged, and R.C. 5301.01 names the officials who can take it: a judge or clerk of a state court of record, the county auditor, the county engineer, a notary public or a mayor. That official certifies the acknowledgment over a signature of their own. Most owners simply visit a notary.

The statutory forms show what a tidy Ohio deed carries. Each names the grantor with marital status and county, recites consideration, gives the grantee's tax-mailing address, describes the land, cites the earlier recorded instrument by volume and page, and includes dower release language for a spouse. The sections reviewed print no separate quitclaim form, so the same elements make a sound checklist for any deed.

One duty trips up sellers of troubled houses. Under R.C. 5301.253, an owner who has received a written building or housing code violation notice must hand the grantee written notice of those violations before any transfer agreement is made, or before the deed is filed if there is no written agreement. A notice sitting on an issuing authority's public records also reaches later owners without a new order.

Where is a deed filed, and what does the recorder charge?

Filing happens with the recorder of the county that holds the parcel, as R.C. 5301.25 directs. Skipping that step leaves a hole: an unrecorded deed is treated as fraudulent against a later buyer who bought in good faith without any knowledge of it.

The recorder's price list sits in R.C. 317.32. The statute prints these items for recording and indexing a standard instrument:

  • Seventeen dollars of base fee and seventeen dollars of housing trust fund fee cover the first two pages.
  • Each page after that adds four dollars of each.
  • A county may tack on a preservation surcharge, capped at five dollars.

The auditor sees the deed first. If a surveyor drew the land, the auditor insists on the surveyor's name appearing in the deed, in a short sentence reading "A survey of this property was made by" and the name.

Who owes the Ohio conveyance fee on a quitclaim?

The party giving up title does. Under R.C. 319.202, the grantor covers the state-set fee plus any county transfer tax when the statement of value reaches the auditor. R.C. 319.54 prices the mandatory fee at one dollar or ten cents for each hundred dollars of value, using whichever is higher.

Counties may layer on a tax of their own. R.C. 322.02 allows up to thirty cents for each hundred dollars, charged to the grantor and handed to the auditor before the deed is taken to the recorder. Ask your auditor whether your county charges it.

How "value" is measured matters. For a sale it means everything paid, mortgage balance included. For a gift in whole or part it means the price the land would likely fetch on the open market. Misstating value on purpose is forbidden. A separate fifty-cent charge covers each transfer or entry on the auditor's books, paid by whoever asks for it.

Which Ohio transfers are exempt from the conveyance fee?

A good number are, and several match the transfers families make by quitclaim. When an exemption fits, the form needs only a note giving the reason.

Selected conveyance fee exemptions in R.C. 319.54(G)(3)
TransferStatute letter
To confirm or correct a deed already recorded(c)
Gift between spouses, or parent and child or the spouse of either(d)
Pursuant to court order, when not a result of a sale under that order(f)
Where no money or other valuable consideration is paid and it is not a gift(m)
Among heirs or devisees of one decedent with no money paid(s)
To a trustee when the grantor reserved an unlimited power to revoke(t)
On sale for delinquent taxes or assessments(e)

The list in section 319.54 runs longer, taking in government transfers, transfers that merely secure or release a debt, and assorted corporate and trust moves.

When do survivorship and transfer on death options beat a quitclaim?

For a family transfer meant to take effect at death, Ohio has statutory tools that a plain quitclaim does not match. R.C. 5302.20 creates survivorship tenancy when a deed or will shows clear intent that the survivor takes the whole. The word "or" between two grantees does not do it alone. A conveyance from fewer than all survivorship tenants to an outsider passes the grantor's interest only on condition that the grantor survives.

A transfer on death designation affidavit under R.C. 5302.22 lets an owner name beneficiaries who take title at death. It requires no payment and no handoff to the beneficiary. It does have to be on file at the recorder's office before the owner dies, at the same recording price as a deed, and it is sworn before someone authorized to administer oaths.

Two more survivorship rules affect family deeds. A conveyance from every survivorship tenant to another person, or from all but one of them to the remaining tenant, ends the survivorship tenancy and vests title in the grantee. And when the only two tenants are spouses and the marriage ends by divorce, annulment or dissolution, the title turns into a tenancy in common unless the judgment says the survivorship continues.

A quitclaim made now gives the grantee a present interest, and the conveyance fee exemptions in the table apply to family gifts. Whatever route is used, no deed clears taxes. The lien statute keeps the year's claim on the parcel until it is paid.

More questions about Ohio Quitclaim Deed

Can I use a quitclaim deed to sell my Ohio house?

Yes, any signed, acknowledged and recorded deed can carry a sale, but a quitclaim gives the buyer only the title you hold, with none of the covenants a warranty form carries. Ask your title company which form the buyer's lender will accept.

Does an Ohio quitclaim deed need to be notarized?

The signature must be acknowledged before one of the officials the statute names, and a notary public is on the list. Most owners use a notary.

Does a quitclaim deed remove a mortgage or tax lien in Ohio?

No. The year's tax lien fastens on the first of January and sticks until paid, whoever holds title. Get payoff numbers from the treasurer and your lender before transferring.

Is there a conveyance fee on a deed between family members?

Gifts between spouses, and gifts from parent to child or a child's spouse, are on the exempt list. So is a transfer where nothing of value changes hands and it is not a gift. The form carries a short statement of the reason.

Where do I record an Ohio quitclaim deed?

Take it to the recorder of the county holding the parcel once the auditor has endorsed it. Until then a later good faith buyer can prevail over it. Ask the recorder's office what it charges for recording.

Ohio transfer on death affidavit FAQ

What is a TOD designation affidavit?

A recorded affidavit that names who receives the property at the owner death under ORC 5302.22.

What is an Ohio transfer on death designation affidavit?

It is a sworn document that names who receives an Ohio home or other real estate when the owner dies, without a probate transfer of that parcel. The authority is Revised Code 5302.22, and the companion rules sit in sections 5302.222 and 5302.23.

The affidavit only works if it is recorded with the county recorder before the owner dies. It does not need a buyer's signature, a payment, or delivery to the person named. Ohio law also says that a transfer made this way is not testamentary, so it takes priority over a will or the intestacy rules for that property.

Owners sometimes mix this up with a transfer on death deed. Ohio's current statute calls the instrument an affidavit, and the older deed form is only mentioned for designations made before the 2009 change.

Who can sign the affidavit and what goes in it?

Sole owners, tenants in common and survivorship tenants may sign, and an owner with a spouse signs jointly with the spouse. The designation may cover the full interest or a stated fraction.

A person authorized to give oaths must verify the signing. Division (D) of section 5302.22 requires the following:

  • A legal description of the land, with a pointer to a recorded instrument containing it.
  • A statement of the exact part being passed, if it is less than everything.
  • The signer's statement that the record shows the signer as owner when the affidavit is recorded, along with marital status.
  • For a married signer, the spouse's statement that dower rights yield to the beneficiary's title.
  • One or more beneficiaries named individually.

A knowingly false statement counts as falsification under division (A)(6) of section 2921.13. The recorder does not draft documents, so most owners hire an attorney or use a title company.

How is the affidavit recorded, and what does it cost?

The owner takes it to the recorder in the county where the land sits. The recorder files it as a deed would be filed, collects the deed fee, and indexes it under the signing owner's name.

Section 317.32 divides each charge between a base fee and a housing trust fund fee. Counties may also levy a document preservation surcharge capped at $5, which makes the final bill county-specific. Get the all-in number from the recorder before sending a check.

Deed-type recording charge, Revised Code 317.32(A)(1) (Ohio Legislative Service Commission)
ComponentFirst two pagesEach later page
Base fee$17$4
Housing trust fund fee$17$4
Preservation surchargeUp to $5 per document, set by the county

Local practice can add a step. Pickaway County's recorder says a transfer on death designation cannot be mailed, because it needs auditor and engineer stamps first and must be carried in.

Does the affidavit change who owns the house while the owner is alive?

No. Section 5302.23 says the designation has no effect on present ownership, and the named beneficiary has no interest in the property until the owner dies. The owner can still sell, mortgage, lease or live in the house.

That matters if you plan to sell. A buyer's title company will see the recorded affidavit in the chain of title, but the owner can convey the property by deed without the beneficiary's consent. Once a deed to a buyer is recorded, the affidavit has nothing left to act on.

The designation also does nothing to lien holders. A mortgagee, judgment creditor or mechanic's lien holder keeps every right it had, and it does not have to name the beneficiary in a foreclosure unless that person holds some other interest in the land.

Can the owner change or revoke the designation?

Yes, at any time and without the beneficiary's consent. The owner records a new transfer on death designation affidavit that states the change, and a later-recorded affidavit supersedes every earlier recorded one for that property.

The statute also builds in several automatic effects:

  • If a named beneficiary dies first and a contingent beneficiary was named, the contingent person takes the same share.
  • If no named beneficiary survives and none is contingent, the interest falls into the owner's probate estate.
  • Several beneficiaries take equal shares as tenants in common unless the affidavit says otherwise or makes them survivorship tenants.
  • If the owner's spouse is the beneficiary and the marriage later ends by divorce, dissolution or annulment, the spouse is treated as having died before the owner.

A recorded affidavit also bars dower rights from vesting in a spouse the owner marries afterward, unless the designation is changed or revoked.

What must the beneficiary file after the owner dies?

The beneficiary signs an affidavit of confirmation. Section 5302.222 has the beneficiary present it to the auditor of the county where the land lies and file it with that county's recorder. A notary or other oath-giver verifies it, and a certified copy of the death certificate goes with it.

Its contents are set by statute: each surviving beneficiary's name and address, the date the owner died, the property description, and the names of any beneficiaries who did not survive. For each of those who died first, a certified death certificate is attached as well.

Land under the Chapter 5309 registration system follows a separate route in section 5309.081. In every case the beneficiary receives only what the owner held at death, along with each mortgage, reservation or exception already tied to the land.

Does a transfer on death transfer carry a conveyance fee?

Frequently it does not, though the auditor makes the call. The list in section 319.54(G)(3) exempts, among others, a transfer where no money or other valuable and tangible consideration changes hands and that is not a gift. For an exempt transfer, section 319.202 asks only for a statement of the reason.

The form family is DTE 100. Paulding County's auditor says DTE 100 (EX) is the one used to claim an exemption, while Pickaway County refuses to transfer anything lacking a completed DTE 100 or DTE 100EX. Check with your own auditor before filing an affidavit of confirmation.

Recording is billed apart from anything the auditor takes, at the same rate as a deed.

Can a house with a recorded affidavit still be sold?

It can. During the owner's life, the owner signs a deed and closing proceeds as usual. Once the owner has died, the beneficiary has to record the affidavit of confirmation before a deed to any buyer will clear the auditor and the recorder.

Skipping an estate for this parcel can save weeks. The beneficiary still carries the mortgage balance, any back property tax, needed repairs and co-owners, because the property arrives burdened by whatever is on record.

An heir who wants to sell an Ohio house as-is for cash should expect the buyer to ask for the recorded affidavit of confirmation first.

More questions about Ohio Transfer on Death Designation Affidavit

Does a transfer on death affidavit keep a house out of probate in Ohio?

For the covered parcel, yes. Section 5302.23 says the transfer is not testamentary and overrides a will or an intestate transfer of that property. A parcel with no surviving named or contingent beneficiary lands in the probate estate.

Does the beneficiary have to sign?

No. Under 5302.22(F) the affidavit needs no payment and no delivery to the beneficiary. It takes effect once recorded with the county recorder during the owner's life.

May an owner name a trust as the beneficiary?

Yes. A beneficiary may be a natural or legal person, such as a bank serving as trustee. If a successor trustee replaces the named trustee before the owner dies, the successor stands in, and the affidavit of confirmation lists that successor.

What happens if the owner was married when signing?

The spouse signs too, and the spouse's dower rights give way to the beneficiary's title. If the spouse is the beneficiary and the marriage later ends by divorce, dissolution or annulment, that designation ends.

Can a lender still foreclose on a house with a recorded affidavit?

Yes. Lienholders keep every right, and the beneficiary inherits subject to existing encumbrances. A lender suing to foreclose need not name the beneficiary unless that person has some other interest in the land.

What we could not confirm

  • County permissive rates by county.

What closing costs does an Ohio seller pay?

An Ohio seller's costs are driven by a few statutory charges plus whatever the purchase contract assigns. The statutory ones are the county auditor's conveyance fee, a possible county transfer tax, a small per-parcel transfer fee and, on paper filings, any recording charge the contract puts on the seller. The rest comes from the contract: payoff of your mortgage and prorations for taxes and similar items.

Ohio law is specific about only some of these. Everything in the table below comes from the Revised Code, so use it as a checklist of the charges the legislature wrote down, and then ask the title agent for the line items on your own closing statement.

Ohio charges set by statute that touch a home sale
ChargeRate as printedSection
Conveyance fee, paid to the county auditor$1 or ten cents per $100 or fraction, whichever is greater319.54(G)(3)
Optional county real property transfer taxUp to thirty cents per $100322.02(A)
Auditor's entry of a land transferFifty cents per transfer319.54(G)(2)
Recording the first two pages of an instrument$17 base plus $17 housing trust fund317.32(A)
Each added page$4 base plus $4 housing trust fund317.32(A)
Optional document preservation surchargeUp to $5 per instrument317.32(A)

Who pays the Ohio conveyance fee?

The grantor, which means the seller. Section 319.202 says the grantor pays the fee under 319.54(G)(3) and any transfer tax levied under Chapter 322 at the time the deed is delivered. Auditor first, recorder second, is the order of stops.

The fee is measured against "value", which the section defines in that section as the full consideration paid or to be paid, including the amount of any mortgage or vendor's lien. For a gift, value means the open-market price between a willing buyer and a willing seller. The law also bars anyone from willfully falsifying the stated value.

Do Ohio counties charge different conveyance rates?

Yes. State law fixes the floor, and commissioners may add a tax of up to thirty cents per hundred dollars under section 322.02. To adopt it, the board must hold two public hearings and publish notice, and the resolution is generally open to a referendum.

Two counties show how the printed figure is expressed. The Morrow County Auditor's page lists $4.00 per thousand for both real estate and manufactured homes. The Muskingum County Auditor's page prints $4.00 per thousand too, calculated by multiplying the sale price by 0.004 and rounding to the nearest ten cents, along with a $0.50 per parcel transfer fee. Other counties publish different numbers, so open your own county auditor's real estate transfer page, or phone the office, before you estimate proceeds.

Which Ohio transfers skip the conveyance fee?

The exemptions in section 319.54(G)(3) matter most to families and estates. Among them:

  • A deed whose sole purpose is to confirm or correct one already recorded.
  • A gift between spouses, or between a parent and a child or that child's spouse.
  • A transfer among heirs at law or devisees of a common decedent when no money is paid.
  • A deed to the trustee of a trust whose maker reserved an unlimited power to revoke.
  • A transfer to or from a person where no money or other valuable consideration is paid and the deal is not a gift.
  • A transfer by court order, as long as it is not the result of a sale made under that order.
  • An interest worth $100 or less.

When a transfer is exempt, the statement of value need only give the reason for the exemption.

How much does recording cost in Ohio?

The recorder's charges come from section 317.32 and are the same set of base and housing trust fund amounts in every county. The statute counts the caption page and any partial page, measured at eight and one-half by fourteen inches, so a deed with exhibits costs more than a short one.

The statute also says fees are due when the instrument is presented, apart from electronic filings, which may be settled afterward by electronic funds transfer or a similar method. It does not say which party to a sale bears the deed's recording cost. Look at your purchase contract, or ask the title agent, to see who is assigned that line.

What happens to the tax bill when an Ohio house closes?

Ohio real estate taxes are billed in two installments, and the Revised Code's default due dates in section 323.12 are December 31 and June 20. Counties set their own closing dates, which can differ.

On a sale, the local treasurer's guidance applies. The Muskingum County Treasurer states that the owner of record receives the bill and that taxes "should be prorated at closing," with the seller crediting the buyer for the prorated share on the closing statement. Other treasurers handle the same process similarly, but a title agent computes the figure.

The deed's statement of value also surfaces two items. If the home received a tax reduction under section 323.152, the statement must address it. If the land was in the Current Agricultural Use Valuation program, a recoupment charge under section 5713.34 may apply when it stops qualifying.

What happens to the seller's mortgage payoff at closing?

The payoff is taken from your proceeds and paid to the lender. The lender then owes a duty under section 5301.36: record a release of the mortgage within ninety days of satisfaction. The statute lets the lender recover the recording fee from the borrower by contract.

If a release is not recorded, the owner can send a written notice, and the lender then has fifteen days before damages of $100 per day begin, capped at $5,000. A mortgagor may also recover $250 in damages for a late release. Check the county recorder's index after closing to confirm it posted.

What disclosures does an Ohio seller owe the buyer?

Anyone selling a home with up to four dwelling units must complete the state's property disclosure form and deliver a signed copy to the buyer, under section 5302.30. The form covers water supply, sewer, structure, hazardous materials and known defects.

A buyer who receives the form after signing the contract can rescind within three business days, and no later than the earlier of thirty days after acceptance or closing. Exceptions include court-ordered transfers, estate fiduciary transfers, and a seller who inherited the home and has not lived there in the past year. If a buyer is borrowing, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau explains that the lender must provide a Closing Disclosure three business days before closing, and its seller-side lines cover credits and prorations.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What does an Ohio seller get back at closing?

A closing statement runs in two directions. Besides charges, a seller can be owed money, most often a refund of taxes or other items prepaid beyond the closing date. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's explainer describes how the buyer's Closing Disclosure shows costs the seller prepaid that the buyer reimburses, and prior taxes and fees the seller owes that the buyer will pay later and the seller covers now. Those lines are where tax prorations land.

The same explainer notes that a seller may agree to contribute to the buyer's closing costs, either as a general amount or as named "Seller Paid" items. If you offer a credit to win a sale, ask for the figure to appear on the contract and on the final statement so it matches.

The net you carry away is the sale price less the payoff, the statutory fees above, any agreed credits and the tax proration. Ask the title agent for a draft statement several days before closing so you can compare each line against the table on this page and the county's printed rate.

More questions about Ohio Closing Costs

What is the Ohio conveyance fee?

It is $1 or ten cents per hundred dollars of value, whichever is greater, under Revised Code 319.54(G)(3). A county may add up to thirty cents per hundred more, and the seller pays both.

Does Ohio have a state transfer tax?

Ohio's charge is collected by the county auditor, not as a single flat state rate. The statutory fee has a floor, and counties may levy an optional tax with a ceiling of thirty cents per hundred dollars.

Who pays recording fees on an Ohio sale?

The statute sets the amount but does not assign it. The purchase contract decides, so check the settlement statement or ask the title agent which side carries the deed's recording fee.

How soon must a lender record a mortgage release in Ohio?

Within ninety days after the mortgage is satisfied. If it is late, the owner can give written notice, and the lender then has fifteen days to record before daily damages start.

Are inherited-house sales exempt from the Ohio disclosure form?

Sometimes. The property disclosure statute exempts a seller who got the property by inheritance and has not lived in it within the past year, as well as transfers by estate fiduciaries.

Ohio tax lien FAQ

Can I stop a tax foreclosure?

Paying the delinquent amount or selling before the sale can pay the tax from the proceeds. Ask the county treasurer for exact figures.

How does unpaid Ohio property tax become a lien?

It is a lien from the first day of each tax year. R.C. 323.11 says the state's lien for the real property tax attaches on January 1 and continues until the tax, penalties, interest and charges are paid. The bill does not arrive until later, but the claim on the parcel already exists.

The lien is why an unpaid balance cannot be left behind at a closing. If only part of a tract is transferred, the same section allows the tax to be apportioned, and the lien then reaches each part only up to the amount allocated to it.

The county treasurer, through the prosecuting attorney, files the foreclosure case, and the owner gets several chances to pay before the property is sold.
