When does an Ohio county start tax foreclosure?

The treasurer may sue once taxes remain unpaid for sixty days after the delinquent land duplicate is delivered to the treasurer. R.C. 323.25 lets the treasurer enforce the lien by civil action the way a mortgage is foreclosed, in the common pleas court, in a municipal court with jurisdiction, or before the county Board of Revision where that board has authority.

A second route sits in R.C. 5721.18. The prosecuting attorney files in the name of the treasurer once the auditor delivers the delinquent land certificate or master list. An in rem action, one against the parcel itself, may be filed after the end of the second year from the date the delinquency was first certified.

The treasurer cannot enforce the lien while any of these applies:

  • The parcel is the subject of a pending application for exemption and is not on the delinquent land duplicate.
  • A valid delinquent tax contract is in force and has not been voided.
  • A tax certificate on the parcel has been sold, as to the taxes it covers.

What can I do to stop a tax foreclosure in Ohio?

Pay the delinquency, or arrange a plan. R.C. 323.31 entitles an owner who lives in the home, or a land contract buyer who occupies it, to at least one written delinquent tax contract with the treasurer, so long as no tax lien certificate or foreclosure judgment is outstanding. Residential contracts last up to five years, and at least two years if the owner asks. Later contracts are at the treasurer's discretion.

The statute lets the contract be signed any time before the adjudication of foreclosure. It breaks if an installment is missed or the current taxes go unpaid, and the prosecuting attorney then files the foreclosure. If a tax certificate was sold, the owner uses a redemption payment plan under section 5721.38 instead.

The right to redeem stays open for a while after suit is filed. R.C. 5721.25 lets any person entitled to redeem pay the taxes, assessments, penalties, interest, charges and costs to the treasurer before foreclosure starts. After filing, redemption is still possible until the entry confirming the sale, or until the alternative redemption period ends, but the owner must also show the property meets zoning, land use, building, health and safety codes. A delinquent tax contract can even be signed after filing, up to five years, though the case keeps moving and the contract can end if the property falls out of code compliance.

What is the alternative redemption period and abandoned land?

It is a short window after judgment. R.C. 323.65 defines it as twenty-eight days after the adjudication of foreclosure is journalized, ending on and including the twenty-eighth day. When it expires, the owner's right and equity of redemption end without a further order. A county treasurer chooses whether to invoke it under section 323.78.

If it is invoked and a city, township, county, school district, community development organization or land reutilization corporation has asked for the parcel, the court or board orders the property deeded to that body without appraisal or sale, free of the taxes and other liens. If nobody asked, the parcel is sold as usual, and if no one bids it is forfeited to the state.

The expedited process for abandoned land is built on the word unoccupied. The statute treats a parcel as unoccupied when no taxable building is lived in, no trade or business is active there, or the parcel is uninhabited with no sign of a change of tenants or improvements. A presumption arises if the parcel is not agricultural and at least two of these hold at certification:

  • No person, trade or business is visibly present at an exterior inspection by the county, municipality or township.
  • No utility connections serve it, or none are being billed.
  • It is boarded up or sealed after being found open, vacant or vandalized.
  • It is insecure, vacant or vandalized on visible inspection.

How do the stages compare, and what happens at the tax sale?

The table lines up the main stages of a county tax foreclosure.

Stages of Ohio delinquent land tax enforcement
StageKey ruleSection
Lien attachesJanuary 1 of each tax year323.11
Suit by treasurerAfter 60 days from delivery of delinquent duplicate323.25
Answer in an in rem actionWithin 28 days after service is complete5721.18
Payment planUp to 5 years for an owner-occupied home323.31
Alternative redemption28 days after judgment is journalized323.65
Second sale if no bidNot less than 2 or more than 6 weeks later5721.19

In an in rem case the answer deadline matters most: section 5721.18 says a default judgment may be taken on any parcel without an answer, and it binds everyone with an interest in it, including those out of state.

Under R.C. 5721.19, the court may order a parcel sold without appraisal for not less than the lesser of two figures: the auditor's fair market value plus costs, or the total amount found due plus costs. If no bid reaches that figure, the sale is adjourned to a second date. If a sale brings less than what is owed, the court may enter a deficiency judgment against the owner of record. A sale in an in rem case under division (B) leaves the buyer with title free of most liens, apart from a properly filed federal tax lien and earlier easements and covenants.

What if I sell the house or money is left after the sale?

Selling does not end a case already filed. R.C. 5721.18(D) says a conveyance after the complaint is filed, and before the foreclosure judgment, does not nullify the county's right to proceed. Ask the treasurer and the prosecuting attorney for a payoff figure that includes the costs of the case, have it paid from the proceeds at closing, and get written confirmation that the case is resolved.

A sale of land for delinquent taxes carries no auditor's conveyance fee under R.C. 319.54, which lists transfers on sale for delinquent taxes among its exemptions.

When a foreclosure sale brings more than the judgment, R.C. 5721.20 sends the excess to the clerk of court within forty-five days after confirmation. The clerk notifies the owner. If the owner does not claim it within ninety days of the final notice, it goes to the county treasury, where the treasurer holds it for three years. After that it is forfeited to the delinquent tax and assessment collection fund, or to a land reutilization fund where the county has one.

More questions about Ohio Tax Liens and Tax Foreclosure

How long can I be behind on Ohio property tax before foreclosure?

The treasurer may sue sixty days after the delinquent land duplicate is delivered. A prosecuting attorney in rem action can follow after the second year from first certification. Ask the treasurer where your parcel stands.

Can I set up a payment plan for delinquent Ohio taxes?

Yes. An owner who lives in the home is entitled to at least one delinquent tax contract, up to five years, or two if requested. No tax lien certificate or foreclosure judgment can be outstanding when the first contract is signed.

Can I still pay after the county files a tax foreclosure?

Yes. You can redeem by paying everything due plus costs before the entry confirming the sale, or before the alternative redemption period of twenty-eight days after judgment ends. The property must also meet local building and zoning codes.

What does the alternative redemption period mean?

It is the twenty-eight days after the court or Board of Revision journalizes the foreclosure judgment. When it ends, the owner's right of redemption is over with no further order. Only counties whose treasurer invokes it use it.

Do I get money back if my house sells for more than the taxes owed?

Yes, excess proceeds go to the clerk, who notifies the owner. If it is unclaimed within ninety days of the final notice, it is held by the county treasurer, and the owner may demand it within three years.

Does every Ohio estate have to go through full probate?

No. Ohio lets a probate court release a small estate from administration, and it provides an even simpler route for the tiniest ones. Which route fits depends on the value of the estate's assets, who inherits, and whether a will exists.

Under R.C. 2113.03, an estate may be released from administration if its assets are worth thirty-five thousand dollars or less. The ceiling is one hundred thousand dollars where the surviving spouse takes everything, either because the will leaves every asset to a spouse named in it, or because there is no valid will and the spouse is entitled to all assets under the intestacy statute.

An interested party applies. The court gives notice to the surviving spouse and heirs, publishes notice in a newspaper of general circulation in the county unless notices are waived or found unnecessary, and, once satisfied, can order personal property delivered and real property transferred to the people entitled to it. If the assets are not all cash and securities with readily known values, an appraiser chosen by the applicant and approved by the court sets the value. The court may also appoint a commissioner to sign the conveyance papers, including those for a sale of real property under R.C. 2127.011.

What is a summary release from administration in Ohio?

R.C. 2113.031 covers the smallest estates. A person who is not the surviving spouse and who paid or is obligated in writing to pay the funeral and burial expenses can apply when the assets do not exceed the lesser of five thousand dollars or those expenses. A surviving spouse can apply when funeral costs were prepaid, or when the spouse paid them, and the assets stay within the support allowance plus up to five thousand dollars for funeral and burial expenses.

The application must be on the form the Ohio Supreme Court prescribes, signed before a notary or a deputy clerk of the probate court, and it must describe every known asset. Vehicle details, bank account numbers and balances, and stock or bond information have to be spelled out. An application for a certificate of transfer goes along with it if the estate holds an interest in real estate, together with the filing fee.

A granted order relieves the estate from administration, directs delivery of personal property with title, and directs transfer of title to any real property interests to the applicant.

Who can sell an inherited Ohio house, and how?

Authority depends on how the estate is handled. When an executor or administrator has been appointed, sales of land follow R.C. 2127.01 through 2127.43. Where the will gives the executor a testamentary power of sale, the executor may use those sections or proceed under the will.

Heirs and devisees who receive the house instead take title through a certificate of transfer under R.C. 2113.61. The executor or administrator files the application after the inventory lists the real property and before the final account. It states the decedent's name, domicile and date of death, whether there was a will, why the property is going to the devisees, whether spousal elections, disclaimers or assignments were filed, and that known debts are paid or secured. Within five days after a compliant application, the court issues the certificate for recording in each county where the land lies.

If no administration happens, an heir or devisee can file the application in the probate court of the county where the decedent lived or where the land sits. When an estate is released from administration, the court's transfer order can substitute for the certificate.

How long do creditors have to present claims against an Ohio estate?

Six months from the date of death. Under R.C. 2117.06, all claims must be presented within six months after death, whether or not the estate is released from administration or an executor or administrator is appointed in that period. A claim presented late is forever barred as to all parties, apart from contingent claims handled under R.C. 2117.37 to 2117.42.

Claims go in writing to the executor or administrator, to that person's attorney of record, or to the probate court with the case number on it. After appointment, the executor or administrator allows or rejects a claim within thirty days of presentation, though a late answer does not hurt the claimant.

This matters to anyone planning a quick sale. The statute on small-estate releases says transfers under an order are made subject to the creditor-claim limits in R.C. 2117.06(B) and (C). A court order relieving the estate has the same effect as administration in freeing real property held by an innocent purchaser for value from claims of unsecured creditors.

Probate court forms, filing fees and local practice vary by county. Ask the clerk of the probate court in the county where the decedent lived for the current checklist.

Can an Ohio owner avoid probate for the house, and what about disclosure and estate tax?

Yes, one route is a transfer on death designation. Under R.C. 5302.22, an owner can record a transfer on death designation affidavit naming beneficiaries. The affidavit is verified before a person authorized to administer oaths, recorded with the county recorder before the owner's death, and needs no consideration and no delivery to the beneficiary. At death, title vests in the beneficiary who survives. A married owner's spouse signs a statement subordinating dower rights.

Disclosure rules matter to a sale from an estate. R.C. 5302.30 exempts transfers ordered by a court, including a probate court, and transfers by a fiduciary in the course of administering an estate. It also exempts a seller who inherited or took by devise and has not lived in the home within the past year. Other sellers of one-to-four unit homes, such as an heir who moved in, must complete the state disclosure form.

On estate tax, R.C. 5731.02 levies the tax on persons dying on or after July 1, 1968 and before January 1, 2013. The levy is limited to those dates.

  • Before any sale, find out which document gives authority: letters from the court, a certificate of transfer, or an order releasing the estate.
  • Ask the probate clerk whether the estate needs a commissioner or an appraisal.
  • Ask the title company which recorded papers it wants to see before closing.

More questions about Ohio Probate Process

What is the Ohio probate limit for a small estate?

Thirty-five thousand dollars or less in assets, or one hundred thousand dollars or less when a surviving spouse takes everything. These figures come from R.C. 2113.03, and the probate court must still enter an order.

How long do creditors have to file claims after a death in Ohio?

Six months after the date of death. A claim not presented in that time is barred, with limited exceptions for contingent claims, under R.C. 2117.06.

Can I sell an inherited Ohio house before probate is finished?

A sale needs someone with authority to convey. That is an appointed executor or administrator, an heir holding a certificate of transfer, or a court-appointed commissioner after a release from administration. Ask the probate court which applies to your estate.

Do I need the Ohio property disclosure form when selling an inherited house?

Not if the transfer is by a fiduciary administering the estate, ordered by a court, or made by an heir or devisee who has not occupied the home within the past year. R.C. 5302.30(B)(2) lists these exemptions.

Does Ohio still have an estate tax?

The levy in R.C. 5731.02 covers deaths before January 1, 2013. Ask the Ohio Department of Taxation about any later-year obligations for a specific estate.
